newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kinshasa rejects Mobutu, upbeat on Kabila -- poll.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa rejects Mobutu, upbeat on Kabila -- poll.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko's popularity has plunged to a two-year low, five months after the start of the rebellion in the east, according to an opinion poll conducted in Zaire's sprawling capital Kinshasa.

The same poll, dismissed by critics as unrepresentative of the nation as a whole, showed over half those questioned had "a good opinion" of rebel leader Laurent Kabila -- but few said they would ever vote for him.

The Zaire-based consulting company, BERCI, which conducted the poll this month and describes itself as independent, said that almost 73 per cent of those questioned had a "bad opinion" of Zaire's ruler of 31 years.
"President Mobutu's image has suffered considerable erosion. Those with a good opinion of Marshal Mobutu have gone from 29 percent in December to 13 percent in March," BERCI said.
Mobutu, 66, seized power in a 1965 military coup.

He is currently at his villa in the South of France. He had prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August and has spent most of his time in Europe since then. A prominent supporter predicted on Friday that he would return on Monday.

The poll said the majority of those questioned felt Mobutu had failed to deliver on a pledge made during a visit in December to resolve the crisis in the east. "For almost 88 percent of those questioned, the head of state has not responded to the expectations raised during his speech," it said.

Critics said the capital, with a population estimated around five million, was a traditional hotbed of opposition to Mobutu, and not representative of nationwide opinion. Mobutu's support has traditionally been much stronger outside the capital.
Tutsi-led rebels who took up arms in October vowing to topple Mobutu hold a vaste swathe of eastern Zaire after meeting little resistance from the notoriously undisciplined army.
Only 13.6 percent of those polled believed that the army was capable of recapturing territory from the rebels.
Kabila, a native of the southern copper-rich province of Shaba, has seen his forces pile victory upon victory.

"Almost 51 percent of those questioned have a good opinion of the rebel leader," the BERCI poll analysis said. "Laurent Kabila constitutes the major beneficiary of Zairean public opinion for the actions by the Tutsi and Banyamulenge revolt."

Migrants from regions affected by the war had a lower opinion of him -- "61 percent of natives of Bandundu trust Kabila, against 27 percent from Shaba, and 28 percent from upper Zaire, two regions suffering from the effects of the war."
BERCI first experimented with opinion polls in Kinshasa in 1991, but stopped political polling until 1995 after insecurity and army-led looting in the capital frightened interviewees.
Olivier Kamitatu, a BERCI director, said it funded political research from market research for Zaire-based businesses.
It conducts polls every two months with face-to-face interviews at home. It says its margin of error is one percent.
In March, it interviewed 1,000 people from 22 districs from a broad cross-section of society.
Only four percent of those questioned said they would vote for Kabila in presidential elections. Paradoxally 56.6 percent disapproved of armed struggle as a means of taking power.
The poll suggested radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi would win an immediate presidential election with 38.5 percent of the vote. Kinshasa is his stronghold.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo came in for an even greater battering than Mobutu -- 88.7 percent had a bad opinion of him.
